cold-war-loans-reward-punish.implications: US officials used their votes and influence at the lenders to cut credit to governments they opposed and open it to governments they backed, so a country's politics could affect whether it got a loan. The clearest record is Chile, where Export-Import Bank, Inter-American Development Bank and World Bank credit fell or stopped under Allende while military aid was not cut. How much of the World Bank's halt came from US pressure, and how much from the Bank's own view of Chile's finances and expropriations, is disputed. Peer-reviewed studies support a link only with limits, and they do not show that the US directly instructed IMF staff.
cold-war-loans-reward-punish.overlap: Partial, with intel-contractors-lenders: both use the 1966 Rusk paper on Indonesia aid through the IMF and World Bank, and lending to the Philippines under martial law. The Chile, Brazil, Nicaragua and voting-study material is new.

odious-debt-dictators.implications: When a dictator borrows and the money is wasted or stolen, the governments that follow can still be made to repay it: the Philippines finished paying P64.7 billion for the Bataan nuclear plant in 2007, though the plant never produced electricity. 'Odious debt' is not an established rule of international law, and relief has come through other routes. Iraq's write-off went through the usual talks among creditor governments (the Paris Club), and Ecuador stopped paying on the strength of its own audit, with no court ruling the bonds illegitimate. Several figures rest on campaign groups or estimates that were not checked against official data, and the studies of money leaving the country (capital flight) show an association, not that each loan was stolen.

why.bataan-nuclear-plant-debt: Named: Bataan plant, Marcos government, US Export-Import Bank, paid off April 2007.
why.ecuador-2008-debt-audit-default: Named: Ecuador's 2007-2008 audit commission, stopped payment on bonds, 2009 buyback at 35 cents.

inflated-forecasts-insiders.implications: The lenders' own reviews show forecasts and pressure to lend running ahead of results: the World Bank's 1992 Wapenhans report linked a rise in problem projects to an "approval culture", and Pakistan's 1994 power policy assumed faster demand growth than came, leaving surplus capacity. Whether Pakistan's surplus came from inflated forecasts or from slower growth is not settled, and IMF research on over-optimistic growth forecasts is mixed. IMF economist Davison Budhoo said the Fund overstated Trinidad and Tobago's labour costs; a government committee found the IMF's figure even more inflated, and the IMF denied any error. John Perkins's claim of a deliberate scheme rests on his own word: records confirm only the outline of his career at Chas. T. Main, and the crash inquiries in Panama and Ecuador found no sabotage.

why.trinidad-1989-austerity: Trinidad and Tobago: the pattern's IMF dispute (1985-89) and its note on the 1989-90 IMF loans after public wage cuts; same lender, years and program.
why.indonesia-may-1998: Not a forecast case. Via Stiglitz's listed claim on IMF pressure to end fuel subsidies in Indonesia, supported for fuel by the January 1998 letter of intent in the pattern's sources; the case is the 1998 fuel price rises under that program.
why.thailand-imf-1997-closures: Not a forecast case. Via Stiglitz's listed claim on IMF austerity in East Asia in 1997-98, naming Thailand; the case is that 1997-98 Thai program. One insider's account, not independently tested in the pattern.

inflated-forecasts-insiders.overlap: Yes, with intel-contractors-lenders: Perkins's 2004 book and Chas. T. Main, Einar Greve, the 1981 Roldós and Torrijos crashes and inquiries, and the State Department's 2006 response. The forecast evidence (Wapenhans, Budhoo, Pakistan, Paiton, IMF forecast studies) and JECOR are new.

economists-pipeline.implications: Economists trained in the United States went on to run finance ministries, central banks and planning agencies while their countries took IMF and World Bank programs, as in Chile after 1973 and Indonesia after 1966. From the 1980s US-based advisers also worked inside governments, including Bolivia, Poland and Russia. In the Russia work, a 2004 ruling found that Harvard advisers Shleifer and Hay broke conflict-of-interest rules, and in 2005 Harvard and both men agreed to pay without admitting liability. Whether foreign training caused these policies or local politics did is argued, not settled, and Bolivian writers dispute that Sachs helped draft Bolivia's 1985 decree.

why.bolivia-tin-miners-1985-1986: Named: Decree 21060 of 29 August 1985 and Sachs's advisory role in Bolivia.
why.russia-mass-privatization-mortality: Covered: USAID's Russian privatization program and the Russian Privatization Center, 1992-94, where HIID worked.
why.argentina-december-2001: Named: Cavallo resigned on 19 December 2001 after the deposit freeze, the event at the centre of this case.

washington-hold-on-imf-world-bank.implications: The United States holds 16.49% of IMF votes, enough to block major policy decisions alone, though day-to-day decisions such as approving a single loan program need only 50%. By informal agreement every permanent World Bank president has been a US citizen and an American holds the IMF's number two post. Treasury officials took part directly in some large rescues, such as Mexico in 1995 and Korea in 1997. The studies show statistical links, not orders from Washington, with one finding broad IMF autonomy outside important, vulnerable countries, and whether Washington pressed for the size of Argentina's 2018 loan is not established here.

why.argentina-imf-standby-2018: Named: Argentina's 2018 IMF stand-by, its largest ever.
why.mexico-1995-austerity: Named event: the 1995 Mexico rescue; the case is the IMF stand-by and austerity package in that rescue.
why.korea-1998-layoff-law-union-arrests: Covered: Lipton's December 1997 test of Kim Dae-jung on labour-market reforms; the case is the February 1998 layoff law.
why.hyundai-ulsan-layoffs-1998: Covered: 1998 Hyundai layoffs under the same labour-market reforms Lipton raised, in the same Korean IMF program.
why.indonesia-may-1998: Covered: the link on senior Treasury involvement in Indonesia's IMF talks, 1997-98; the case is that program in May 1998.
why.argentina-december-2001: Covered: the link on the State Department and NSC pushing to extend IMF loans to Argentina in 2001; the case is the end of that lending.

washington-hold-on-imf-world-bank.overlap: Partial, with companies-come-from: both state the 16.49% US vote, the 85% rule and the custom of a US World Bank president. That is one passage in companies-come-from; the Treasury episodes and voting studies are new.

revolving-door-wall-street-lenders.implications: The top jobs at the IMF and World Bank are filled largely by people moving between finance ministries or central banks, private banks and funds, and back. Alden Clausen, for example, went from Bank of America to the World Bank presidency and back, and Stanley Fischer went from the IMF's number two post to Citigroup. Two former IMF heads were later convicted in separate matters: Rato over company credit cards and, in 2024, over tax crimes, money laundering and corruption, which he said he would appeal; and Lagarde of negligence over an arbitration award, with no penalty. These records show where people worked; no source checked here ties a specific IMF or World Bank decision to a later private job.

rescue-loans-paid-foreign-lenders.implications: In crises from 1995 to 2018, emergency money from the IMF, the US Treasury, European governments and the European Central Bank arrived while foreign banks and bondholders were pulling money out, and it helped keep debts paid on time. That let many private lenders reduce how much they stood to lose, and part of the debt moved onto the public books of the borrowing country and its official lenders. The IMF's own 2013 evaluation says this happened in Greece after 2010. The record is not uniform: many foreign investors in Mexico still took large losses, Russia froze part of its debt after an IMF payment, Nordic parent banks pledged to maintain their overall exposure (the money they had at risk) in Latvia, and who gained most from the 2010 Greek programme is disputed.

why.mexico-1995-austerity: Named rescue: Mexico 1995; the case is the IMF stand-by and tax and price package within it.
why.korea-1998-layoff-law-union-arrests: Same rescue: Korea's IMF stand-by of 4 December 1997; the case is a labour condition of that program.
why.hyundai-ulsan-layoffs-1998: Same rescue: Korea's IMF stand-by of 4 December 1997, the arrangement this case cites.
why.thailand-imf-1997-closures: Named: foreign bank claims on Thailand fell between June 1997 and December 1998, under its IMF program; the case is that program.
why.indonesia-may-1998: Same rescue: Indonesia's IMF arrangement of 5 November 1997; the case is its May 1998 review and fuel price rises.
why.brazil-1999-imf-social-cuts: Named rescue: Brazil's December 1998 package; the case is the budget cuts under it.
why.argentina-december-2001: Named: IMF arrangement raised to $22bn in 2001; the case is the end of that support.
why.greece-may-2010-strike-marfin: Named rescue: Greece 2010; the case is the May 2010 package and the strike against it.
why.greece-pension-cuts: Same rescue: pension cuts under the May 2010 Greek package and its memoranda.
why.greece-health-spending-cap: Same rescue: health spending cap under the 2010 Greek programme's memoranda.
why.greece-2012-bailout-austerity: Covered: the Rocholl and Stahmer claim on Greek money to June 2015, including the 2012 restructuring; the case cites the same paper.
why.ireland-bailout-austerity-2010: Named rescue: Ireland's 2010 EU-IMF package; the case is its memorandum.
why.ireland-water-charges: Same rescue, harm not named in the text: water charges were written into the memorandum of the 2010 EU-IMF package. Charges began in October 2014, after the program ended.
why.latvia-riga-riot-2009: Same rescue: Latvia's December 2008 IMF and EU package; the case is its budget cuts. The text uses Latvia as a counter-case on bank withdrawals.

investors-sue-after-privatization.implications: Investment treaties let foreign companies that bought or ran privatized services sue governments that froze tariffs, changed contracts or took services back, most often at ICSID, the World Bank Group's arbitration centre. Results vary: Argentina, the main target, faced awards such as $405m to Suez and its partners, while the Biwater tribunal awarded $0, Bechtel dropped its claim and Veolia's claim against Egypt was dismissed. Two of the water deals, in Bolivia and Tanzania, were themselves tied to the World Bank. Some Argentine awards were later annulled or settled for less, and the total Argentina actually paid is not established.

why.cochabamba-water-war: Named: Bechtel's Aguas del Tunari contract, ended April 2000, claim dropped 2006.
why.dar-es-salaam-water: Named: Biwater's City Water, ended May 2005, tribunal awarded $0 in 2008.
why.buenos-aires-aguas-argentinas: Named: the Buenos Aires water case, $405m award to Suez and co-claimants in 2015.

investors-sue-after-privatization.overlap: Yes, substantially, with company-sued-the-state: same mechanism and ICSID's World Bank tie, and the same Cochabamba, Dar es Salaam, Buenos Aires and Tucumán disputes. New here: the wider Argentine crisis claims and the 2013 bond settlement, Urbaser, Veolia, Occidental and Vattenfall. Both Buenos Aires claim figures are press figures for the same claim; the award records the four owners' total as $1,019.2m in June 2008 and $868m at the end. See r19f_pats_fixes.json.

imf-lending-waves.implications: The number of countries under an IMF arrangement rose and fell over time, reaching a peak of 75 in 1996. The map colours each country by the period in which it spent the most years under arrangements, though many countries were under programs in several waves. This is the map's own count of arrangements, leaving out emergency and rapid payouts, and it does not show what the loans did in any country.

sold-then-taken-back.implications: From 1988 to 2008 the World Bank recorded 10,193 sales and handovers of state firms and services in 124 low- and middle-income countries, and from 2000 the Public Futures database records 1,787 cases of services taken back or newly made public. In 55 countries, services were sold and some were later taken back. The two records were made differently: the World Bank's counts sales with a price in poorer countries only, while Public Futures relies on reported cases worldwide. A take-back does not always reverse the same sale, and a country with no take-back recorded may still have had some.

price-protests-and-programs.implications: Of 1,414 protests over price rises and taxes coded from 1990 to 2020, 487 took place in a country and year with an IMF arrangement in force and 927 outside one. This shows timing only: a protest during a program year was not necessarily about the program. Countries under IMF programs are often already in economic crisis, which raises prices on its own, and this count cannot separate the two. The data come from a set of major newspapers, so smaller protests and those in less-covered countries are missed.

imf-conditions-waves.implications: The number of conditions the IMF wrote into its loans each year rose through the 1980s and 1990s and peaked in 1996, at 2,983 worldwide. The map colours each country by the decade in which it received the most conditions. This is a count only: it does not say what the conditions required or what they did in any country.
